A nodemailer Transport, and Mailpit

config/mailer.js: one shared SMTP transport, pointed at a local Mailpit container instead of a real mail server or an external dev-inbox provider.

nodemailer needs to know one thing to send a message at all: which SMTP server to hand it to. That's a transport, configured once and shared — the same import-as-singleton idiom config/db.js and this lesson's events/emitter.js already used:

// Figure 5.10: one shared SMTP transport (src/config/mailer.js)
import nodemailer from 'nodemailer';
import env from './env.js';

const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: env.MAIL_HOST,
  port: env.MAIL_PORT,
  secure: false,
});

export default transport;

host/port point at Mailpit, a small SMTP server that runs locally in Docker for exactly this purpose: it accepts a real SMTP conversation on port 1025 — so nodemailer genuinely believes it's talking to a mail server — but instead of relaying anything onward, it just keeps every message and shows it in a web UI at localhost:8025. Nothing sent through it ever reaches a real inbox or leaves the machine, which is exactly what local development wants: real enough to catch a broken email (wrong recipient, malformed template) without any risk of accidentally spamming a real address while testing.

# Figure 5.11: Mailpit as a docker-compose service (docker-compose.yml, excerpt)
mailpit:
  image: axllent/mailpit:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  ports:
    - '1025:1025' # SMTP — nodemailer's transport target
    - '8025:8025' # web UI — http://localhost:8025

MAIL_HOST/MAIL_PORT join config/env.js's Zod schema alongside MAIL_FROM, all three defaulted to match this compose service, so npm run dev works against a freshly started mailpit container with no .env changes required. Swapping to a real provider later — for an actual deployment — is purely a matter of pointing these same three env vars at it; nothing in mailer.js or any listener would need to change.
